chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: ANTIGONE and ISMENE before the Palace gates.

ANTIGONE. Ismene, sister of my blood and heart, do you see how Zeus intends to fulfill in our lifetime the curse of Oedipus, a whole world of misery? What pain, what affliction, what outrage or shame is missing from the fortunes you and I share? And now this proclamation made today by our Captain-General to the whole state — what can it mean? Did you hear and take it in, or are you deaf to the news that our own are branded as enemies?

ISMENE. To me, Antigone, no word about our family has come, neither glad nor grievous, since the two of us lost our two brothers in a single day by their double fratricide. And since the Argive army fled in the night, no later news has reached me, for better or worse.
ANTIGONE. I knew it, and that is why I summoned you outside the gates — so I could say it in your ear alone.
ISMENE. What is it? Some dark secret is stirring in you.

ANTIGONE. What else but the fate of our two dead brothers? Creon has given one the honor of burial rites and denied the other. Eteocles, so they say, he has laid in the ground with the customary ceremonies, honored among the dead below. But Polyneices, a dishonored corpse — so the royal edict is said to run — no man may bury him or mourn for him. He must be left without a tomb and without tears, a feast for kites to scent from far away and swoop down upon. That is the edict, if the report is true, of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed at you and me — yes, me too. And soon he will be here to proclaim his order to anyone who hasn't heard it. This is no passing whim. The edict says that whoever breaks it shall be stoned to death. That is where we stand. Now it's for you to show whether you are worthy of your blood or unworthy.
ISMENE. But how, my rash and loving sister, can I do anything at all to make or mar this?
ANTIGONE. Say whether you will help me and stand with me. Decide.
ISMENE. In what bold venture? What are you thinking?
ANTIGONE. Lend me a hand to carry the corpse away.
ISMENE. What — bury him despite the prohibition?
ANTIGONE. He is my brother, and yours too, though you deny him. No one will say that I betrayed a brother.
ISMENE. Will you persist, even though Creon has forbidden it?
ANTIGONE. What right has he to keep me from my own?

ISMENE. Think, sister, of our father's fate — hated, dishonored, convicted of sin by his own confession, blinded by his own hand. Think of his mother-wife, those ill-matched names, undone by a noose she herself had twisted. And last, our wretched brothers in a single day, caught in one shared destiny, self-slaughtered, each at once the slayer and the slain. Think, sister, how we are left alone. Shall we not perish most miserable of all if, in defiance of the law, we cross a king's will? We are weak women, remember that — not made by nature to contend with men. And remember too that the stronger rules. We must obey his orders, these or worse. So I plead compulsion and beg the dead to pardon me. I have no choice but to obey the powers that be. It is foolishness, I believe, to overstep the golden mean in anything.

ANTIGONE. I won't press you any longer. No — even if you were willing now, I wouldn't welcome your help. Go your own way. I'll bury him myself. How sweet to die in such a task, to rest — sister and brother locked in love's embrace — a sinless sinner, banished from earth for a little while but commended by the dead. And with them I shall stay for ever. As for you, scorn, if you like, the eternal laws of Heaven.
ISMENE. I do not scorn them. I simply have no skill to defy the State or break her ordinance.
ANTIGONE. A convenient excuse. I will go alone to lay my dearest brother in the grave.
ISMENE. My poor, loving sister, how I fear for you!
ANTIGONE. Oh, waste no fears on me. Look to yourself.
ISMENE. At least let no one know what you intend. Keep it close and secret, as I will.
ANTIGONE. Oh, tell it, sister! I shall hate you more if you do not proclaim it to the whole town.
ISMENE. You have a fiery spirit for such cold, numbing work.
ANTIGONE. I please the ones I most want to please.
ISMENE. If you succeed. But you are doomed to fail.
ANTIGONE. When my strength fails me, yes — but not before.
ISMENE. But if the venture is hopeless, why try at all?

ANTIGONE. Sister, stop, or I shall hate you soon, and the dead man will hate you too, with good reason. Say I am mad, and let my madness run its course. The worst that can happen is that I die an honorable death.
ISMENE. Have it your way then. It is a mad undertaking — yet to those who love you, you are as dear as ever.
[Exeunt]

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: CHORUS. Sunbeam, of all the rays that ever dawn upon our seven-gated Thebes, the brightest of all — O eye of golden day, how fair your light shone over Dirce's fountain, driving the Argive army headlong on their homeward course, far quicker than they came. You put to flight their silver shields, that host with its white-emblazoned bucklers. Against our land the proud invader had come to press the claim of deadly Polyneices. Like an eagle swooping low, on pinions white as new-fallen snow, with a clanging scream, with a horsetail plume for a crest, the aspiring lord of Argos pressed onward.

Hovering around our city walls he waited, his spearmen ravenous at our seven gates. But before a torch could set our crown of towers alight, before they had tasted our blood, they turned — forced back by the Dragon. In their rear they heard the din of Ares striking them with panic. For Zeus, who hates a braggart's boast, watched that gold-bespangled host. As they raised the paean at the goal, he struck them down with the forked blaze of his lightning.

From earth to earth he crashed, rebounding. The firebrand was dashed from his impious hand as he came on like a Bacchic reveler, breathing out hate and flame. And he staggered. Elsewhere on the field, here and there, great Ares wheeled like a war-horse. Beneath his chariot our enemies were thrust down and bit the dust.

Seven captains at our seven gates thundered. For each a champion was waiting. Each left behind his bright armor as a trophy for Zeus, who turns the tide of battle. All but two — that ill-starred pair, born of one mother to one father — who, lance in rest, drove one against the other and both perished, brother slain by brother.

Now Victory returns again to Thebes and smiles upon her chariot-circled plain. Now let feast and festal shouts blot out the memories of war. Let us throng to the temples, dance and sing the whole night through. God of Thebes, lead the round. Bacchus, shaker of the ground! But let us end our revels here — look, Creon our new lord draws near, crowned by this strange turn of fortune, our king. What, I wonder, is he pondering? Why this summons? Why call us, his elders, one and all, bidding us debate with him on some grave concern of state?

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: [Enter CREON]

CREON. Elders, the gods have once again righted our storm-tossed ship of state, now safe in port. But you I have convened by special summons as my most trusted councilors. First, because I knew you were loyal to Laius in the old days. And again, when Oedipus restored our state, you were constant to the royal line both while he ruled and after his rule was over. Now that his two sons have perished in a single day, brother murdering brother, by right of kinship to the dead princes I claim and hold the throne and sovereignty. Yet it is no easy matter to discern the temper of a man, his mind and will, until he has been proved by the exercise of power. In my own case: any ruler at the top who swerves from the highest policy, tongue-tied by fear of consequences, that man I hold, and have always held, the basest of the base. And I despise the man who puts a friend above his country. As for myself, I call Zeus to witness, whose eyes see everything: if I perceive some mischief hatching to undermine the state, I will not hold my tongue. Nor would I count a public enemy as my private friend. I know well that the state is the good ship that holds all our fortunes — and if she wrecks, so does friendship. Such is the policy by which I mean to serve the commonwealth. And in keeping with it, I have proclaimed an edict concerning the sons of Oedipus. Eteocles, who fought and fell as his country's foremost champion in battle — bury him with all the observances and ceremonies that are the reward of heroic dead. But for the miscreant exile who came back bent on wiping out his father's city and his father's gods in flames and ashes, determined to glut his vengeance with his kinsmen's blood or drag them captive at his chariot wheels — for Polyneices it is decreed that none shall give him burial or mourn for him. His corpse is to be left unburied, to be food for dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight. That is my purpose. Never by my will shall villains take precedence over loyal men. Every good patriot, living or dead, will be honored and preferred by me.
CHORUS. Son of Menoeceus, such is your will for both the man who loathed our state and the one who loved it. Your word is law. You may dispose of us the living as you please, and of the dead as well.
CREON. See then that you carry out what I command.
CHORUS. Lay this hard task on younger shoulders.
CREON. Don't worry — I've already posted guards to watch the corpse.
CHORUS. What further duty would you lay on us?
CREON. Not to connive at any disobedience.
CHORUS. No man is mad enough to court his own death.
CREON. Death is indeed the penalty — and yet the hope of profit has often lured men to their ruin.
[Enter GUARD]

GUARD. My lord, I won't pretend I have been panting and running like a swift messenger. The truth is my soul, under its burden of thought, kept making halts and turning back, again and again. Conscience plied the spur and the bridle by turns. "Why hurry headlong to your fate, fool?" it whispered. And then again, "If Creon learns this from someone else, you'll be sorrier yet." So, in a leisurely way, I hurried along the road. Heavy thinking turns a short furlong into a league. But in the end the forward voice won out, and I came to face you. I'll speak, even if I have nothing to say. Plucking courage out of despair, I thought, "Let the worst come. You can only meet your fate."
CREON. What's your news? Why this gloom?
GUARD. Let me first say a word about myself. I didn't do the deed. I didn't see it done. And it wouldn't be fair for me to come to harm for it.
CREON. You parry well, and clearly you're fencing around some matter of grave importance.
GUARD. A man bringing dreadful news is bound to tremble.
CREON. Then, fellow, shoot your bolt and be gone.
GUARD. Well, it has to come out. The corpse has been buried. Someone just now sprinkled it with thirsty dust, performed the proper ritual, and was gone.
CREON. What are you saying? Who has dared to do this thing?

GUARD. I cannot tell. There was no trace of a pick or mattock — hard, unbroken ground, no scratch, no rut of chariot wheels, no sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch gave the alarm, we were all terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished — not buried in the earth, but strewn with dust, as though by someone trying to ward off the curse that haunts the unburied dead. No sign of a dog or a ravening jackal, not a scratch. Then an angry war of words broke out. Guard railed at guard and we were ready to come to blows, with no one to separate us. Each of us in turn was suspected, but nothing could be pinned on any one, for lack of evidence. We challenged each other to the ordeal — to handle red-hot iron or pass through fire, swearing on oath that we had neither done the deed ourselves nor knew who did or contrived it. Our investigation was at a standstill when one man spoke and bowed us all to earth like trembling reeds. There was no answering him and no way to escape our doom. "You are bound to tell the king," he said. "You cannot hide it." And he convinced us all. So lots were cast, and I, the unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am, unwilling and also unwelcome. No one cares to hear bad news.
CHORUS. I had misgivings from the first, my lord, that something more than natural was at work here.

CREON. Oh, stop — you vex me with your babbling. I'm beginning to think you are going senile in your old age. Is it not sheer folly to pretend that the gods would spare a thought for this dead man? Did they award him some special favor and bury him as a benefactor — he who came to burn their hallowed sanctuaries, to sack their shrines, to ravage their land, and to trample their ordinances? Or perhaps the gods bestow their favors on the wicked? No! No! I have long noted the malcontents who wagged their heads and kicked against the yoke, resenting these orders of mine and my rule. It is they, I guarantee it, who have bribed my guards. Of all the evils current on earth, the worst is money. Money sacks cities. Money drives men out from hearth and home. It warps and seduces honest natures and breeds a habit of dishonesty. But those who sold themselves will find their greed has overshot the mark, and they will rue it sooner or later. Yes — as I still revere the dread of Zeus, by Zeus I swear: unless you find and bring before me the very man who carried out this lawless burial, death alone won't be punishment enough. You'll be strung up alive first and made to confess this outrage. That will teach you what practices are apt to pay. There are some villainies that bring no gain. Dishonesty may make a few men rich, but it ruins and disgraces many more.
GUARD. May I speak, or must I turn and go without a word?
CREON. Be off! Can't you see that even this question irks me?
GUARD. Where, my lord? Is it your ears that suffer, or your heart?
CREON. Why try to probe and find the seat of pain?
GUARD. I annoy your ears — the real villain annoys your mind.
CREON. What an incorrigible babbler! Get out!
GUARD. A babbler maybe, but innocent of the crime.
CREON. Twice guilty — having sold your soul for gain.
GUARD. It's a sorry thing when reasoners reason wrongly.
CREON. Go on, quibble with your reason. If you fail to find these criminals, you'll admit that the wages of ill-gotten gain are death.
[Exit CREON]

GUARD. I pray he will be found. But caught or not — and luck must decide that — you will never see me back here again. That much is sure. Past all hope or thought I have escaped, and for my safety I owe the gods much thanks.

chapters.title: First Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Many wonders there are, but nothing more wondrous than man. Over the surging sea, with a whitening south wind pale behind him, through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way. And the eldest of deities, Earth — who knows neither toil nor decay — he furrows and scores year in, year out, turning the plowshare with his team, the breed of the yoked horse.

The light-witted birds of the air, the beasts of the forest and the wild, he traps with his woven snare, and the brood of the briny flood too. A master of cunning: the savage bull, and the stag that roams the mountain free, are tamed by his infinite art. The shaggy, rough-maned steed is broken in to bear the bit.

Speech, and wind-swift thought, and the civic wit to live by counsel — all these he has taught himself. And the arrowy rain to fly from, and the nipping airs that freeze beneath the open winter sky. He has provision for everything. Even grim plague he has learned to endure. He is safe, whatever befalls. Yet for death he has found no cure.

Past the wildest flight of thought are the cunning and skill that lead man now toward the light, now toward evil counsels. If he honors the laws of the land and reveres the gods of the state, proudly his city shall stand. But a cityless outcast I reckon whoever, bold in his pride, departs from the path of right. Never may I sit at his side or share the thoughts of his heart.

What strange vision meets my eyes and fills me with wild surprise? Surely I know her, surely it is she — the maiden Antigone. Hapless child of a hapless father, did you recklessly conspire, madly brave the king's decree? Is that why they are hauling you here?

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
GUARD. Here is the culprit, taken in the act of giving burial. But where is the King?
CHORUS. There — from the palace he returns in time.
[Enter CREON]
CREON. Why is my presence timely? What has happened?

GUARD. My lord, no man should ever make a vow — because the moment he swears he won't do a thing, his second thoughts contradict his first resolve. When I fled the hailstorm of your threats, I swore you would never see me here again. But the wild rapture of this glad surprise intoxicates, and so I'm here, forsworn. And here is my prisoner, caught in the very act, adorning the grave. No lottery this time. This prize is mine by right of treasure-trove. So take her, judge her, rack her, if you will. She is yours, my liege. But I can rightly claim the right to leave, well rid of all these troubles.
CREON. Tell me, how did you arrest the girl, and where?
GUARD. Burying the man. There's nothing more to tell.
CREON. Have you your wits about you? Do you know what you're saying?
GUARD. I saw this woman burying the corpse against your orders. Is that clear and plain enough?
CREON. But how was she caught in the act?

GUARD. It happened this way. No sooner had we come, driven from your presence by those awful threats, than we swept away every trace of dust and bared the clammy body. Then we sat on the ridge upwind of the stench. Each man kept his fellow alert and roundly rated any sluggard who chanced to nap. So all night long we watched, until the sun stood high in heaven and its blazing beams beat down on us. Then suddenly a whirlwind raised a cloud of dust that blotted out the sky, swept the plain, stripped the woodlands bare, and shook the firmament. We closed our eyes and waited until the heaven-sent plague should pass. At last it ceased, and look — there stood this girl. A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill, like a mother bird when she finds her nest robbed of its nestlings. Just so this girl wailed when she saw the body stripped and bare, and cursed the ruffians who had done the deed. Then she gathered handfuls of dry dust, and holding up a finely wrought bronze urn, poured a libation three times over the dead. At the sight we swooped down and seized our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when we charged her with the earlier crime and this one, she denied nothing. I was glad — and grieved. For it is sweet to escape harm yourself, and yet grievous to bring disaster on a friend. All in all, I reckon a man's first duty is to serve himself.
CREON. Speak, girl, with your head bent low and your eyes cast down. Do you plead guilty or deny the deed?
ANTIGONE. Guilty. I did it. I don't deny it.
CREON (to GUARD). Fellow, be off wherever you will, and thank your luck you've escaped a heavy charge. (To ANTIGONE.) Now answer this plain question, yes or no: did you know about the proclamation?
ANTIGONE. I knew. Everyone knew. How could I not know?
CREON. And yet you were bold enough to break the law?

ANTIGONE. Yes — because these laws were not ordained by Zeus, and Justice, who sits enthroned with the gods below, did not establish these human laws. Nor did I think that you, a mortal man, could with a single breath annul and override the immutable, unwritten laws of Heaven. They are not of today or yesterday. They do not die, and no one knows from where they sprang. I was not about, from fear of any man's frown, to disobey these laws and so provoke the wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die, even had you not proclaimed it. And if my death is hastened by this, I count it gain. For death is gain to one whose life, like mine, is full of misery. So my lot seems to me not sad but blessed. If I had endured to leave my mother's son unburied there, I would have grieved with reason — but not now. And if in this you judge me a fool, perhaps the one who calls me foolish is a fool himself.
CHORUS. A stubborn daughter of a stubborn father — this ill-starred girl kicks against the pricks.

CREON. Well, let her know that the most stubborn wills are soonest broken, as the hardest iron, over-heated in the fire to brittleness, flies apart first into fragments, shivered through. A small bit curbs the fieriest horse, and a man who lives in subjection must learn to be meek. But this proud girl, well-schooled in insolence, first overstepped the established law, and then — a second and worse act of insolence — she boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she can flout my authority like this and go unpunished, then I am the woman and she the man. But though she be my sister's child, or closer kin than everyone who worships at my hearth, neither she nor her sister shall escape the ultimate penalty. For I hold both of them equally guilty, as arch-conspirators in this. Bring the older one out — even now I saw her inside the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind often give away dark deeds plotted in darkness before the act. What I hate more still is a criminal caught in the act who tries to make a virtue of the crime.
ANTIGONE. Would you do more than kill your prisoner?
CREON. No — your life is mine, and that is enough.

ANTIGONE. Why dally then? No word of yours is pleasant to me — God forbid it ever should be — nor am I any more acceptable to you. And yet how else could I have won a name as glorious as this — by burying my brother? All my townsmen would say as much, if they weren't gagged by terror. A king has many privileges, and not the least of them is that all his acts and words are law.
CREON. Of all these Thebans, none thinks that way except you.
ANTIGONE. These men think as I do, but they hold their breath in your presence.
CREON. Aren't you ashamed to differ from all of them?
ANTIGONE. To honor my own kin can bring no shame.
CREON. Was his dead enemy not your kinsman too?
ANTIGONE. One mother bore them, and the same father.
CREON. Why cast a slur on the one by honoring the other?
ANTIGONE. The dead man himself would not support you in this.
CREON. Surely he would, if you honor the bad as much as the brave.
ANTIGONE. The one who was killed was no villain — he was a brother.
CREON. The patriot perished by the outlaw's hand.
ANTIGONE. Even so, the realms below require these rites.
CREON. Not that the base should fare the same as the brave.
ANTIGONE. Who knows if this world's crimes are virtues there?
CREON. Not even death can make a foe a friend.
ANTIGONE. My nature is made for mutual love, not hate.
CREON. Die then, and love the dead if you must. No woman shall be master while I live.
[Enter ISMENE]
CHORUS. Look — from out the palace gate, weeping over her sister's fate, comes Ismene. See her brow, once serene, now clouded. See her lovely face flushed with angry red.

CREON. Woman, who like a viper I never saw harbored in my house, draining my blood — two plagues I nurtured blindly, I see it now, to undermine my throne. Say, did you too have a hand in this crime, or do you abjure any part in it?
ISMENE. I did the deed, if she will have it so, and with my sister I claim to share the guilt.
ANTIGONE. That would be unjust. You wouldn't act with me at first, and I refused your partnership.
ISMENE. But now that your boat is stranded, I am bold to claim my share as partner in the loss.
ANTIGONE. Who did the deed, the underworld knows well. A friend in word alone is no friend of mine.
ISMENE. O sister, do not scorn me. Let me share your work of piety, and die with you.
ANTIGONE. Don't claim a work you had no hand in. One death is enough. Why should you die?
ISMENE. What would life profit me without you?
ANTIGONE. Ask Creon. He's your kinsman and your best friend.
ISMENE. Why taunt me? Do you take pleasure in these gibes?
ANTIGONE. It's a sad mockery, if I am mocking at all.
ISMENE. Oh, tell me — can I help you even now?
ANTIGONE. No. Save yourself. I don't begrudge you your escape.
ISMENE. Is even this boon denied me, to share your fate?
ANTIGONE. Yes — because you chose life, and I chose to die.
ISMENE. You cannot say I did not protest.
ANTIGONE. Well, some approved your wisdom, others mine.
ISMENE. But now we stand convicted, both alike.
ANTIGONE. Fear not. You are alive. I died long ago, when I gave my life to save the dead.
CREON. Both girls are crazed, I think. One has suddenly lost her wits, the other was born mad.
ISMENE. Yes, that is how it goes, sire, when misfortune comes. Even the wisest lose their mother wit.
CREON. Indeed your wit deserted you when you chose to do evil with evil-doers.
ISMENE. What life is there for me without my sister?
CREON. Don't say "my sister" — your sister is dead.
ISMENE. What, would you kill your own son's promised bride?
CREON. Aye — let him raise his seed from other fields.
ISMENE. No new betrothal can be like the old.
CREON. A plague on loose girls who court and woo our sons.
ANTIGONE. O Haemon, how your father dishonors you!
CREON. A plague on you and your accursed marriage!

chapters.title: Second Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. What — will you rob your own son of his bride?
CREON. It is Death that bars this marriage, not his father.
CHORUS. So her death-warrant, it seems, is sealed.

CREON. By you, just as it was first by me. Off with them, guards — keep them close. Henceforth let them learn to live as women should, not roam at large. For even the bravest spirits run away when they see death pressing close on life's heels.

CHORUS. Three times blessed are those who have never tasted pain. Once the curse of Heaven infects a bloodline, the infection lingers on and spreads apace, generation after generation, and each must drain the cup.

So when the Etesian winds from Thrace pour down, sweeping over the blackening sea and whirling up onto the land the ooze and sand from Ocean's cavernous depths, billow upon billow thunders on the shore.
On the house of Labdacus I see descending woe upon woe. From ancient days some god laid a curse on the race, and his rod scourges age after age with sorrows that never end.
The light that dawned upon its last-born son is gone, and the bloody axe of Fate has felled the handsome tree that flowered late. O Oedipus, undone by your own reckless pride!

Your might, O Zeus — what mortal power can quell it? Not sleep, that lays everything else beneath its spell, nor the moons that never tire. Untouched by Time, throned in the dazzling light that crowns Olympus' height, you reign as king, omnipotent, sublime.
Past, present, and to come, all bow to your decree. All that exceeds the mean is punished by Fate, whether in love or hate.

Hope flits about on never-tiring wings. To some she brings profit, to some light loves. But no one knows how her gifts may turn until the treacherous ashes burn beneath his feet. It was a wise man, surely, who spoke this word: When evil seems good to any man, Fate is near. And brief is the respite before her flaming sword.
Here comes in an angry mood Haemon, youngest of your brood. Is it for his bride that he is grieved, or for his marriage-bed deceived? Does he mourn for you, maid forlorn, Antigone?

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: [Enter HAEMON]

CREON. We shall know soon, better than any seer can tell. My son — having heard the sealed decree about your bride, you don't mean to rage against your father, do you? Don't you know that whatever we do is done in love?
HAEMON. O father, I am yours, and I will take your wisdom as the helm to steer by. Therefore no marriage shall be held more precious by me than your loving guidance.

CREON. Well spoken. That is how right-minded sons should feel, deferring in everything to a father's will. For it is the hope of parents to rear a brood of sons who will be submissive, eager to avenge their father's wrongs and count his friends their own. But whoever fathers unprofitable sons breeds trouble for himself and much laughter for his enemies. Son, be warned, and don't let a woman fool away your wits. It goes badly for a husband saddled with a shrew — her embraces go cold soon enough. What wound cuts so quickly to the quick as a false friend? So spit her out, cast her off. Let her go find a husband among the dead. Since I have caught her openly rebelling — the one malcontent among all my subjects — I will not prove a traitor to the state. She shall surely die. Let her appeal, if she likes, to Zeus the God of Kindred. For if I nurture rebellion in my own house, won't I foster mutiny outside it too? The man who rules his household well will prove no less wise in civic matters. But whoever overbears the laws, or thinks to overrule his rulers — such a man I will never allow. Whomever the state appoints must be obeyed in everything, in small things and great, in just things and unjust alike. I warrant such a man, in either role, would shine — as king or as subject. Such a man would stand his ground in the storm of battle, a comrade loyal and true. But Anarchy — what evils does Anarchy not work! She ruins states, she overthrows homes, she dissolves and routs armies in the field. Discipline preserves the ordered ranks. Therefore we must maintain authority and never yield to a woman's will. Better, if it must be, that men should cast us out than for it to be said a woman proved our match.
CHORUS. To me, unless old age has dulled my wits, your words seem both reasonable and wise.

HAEMON. Father, the gods implant reason in mortal men — the choicest gift bestowed by heaven. It is not for me to say you are wrong, and I could not arraign your wisdom even if I tried. And yet wise thoughts may come to other men as well, and as your son it falls to me to note the acts, the words, the comments of the crowd. The common people stand in terror of your frown and dare not utter anything that might offend. But I can overhear their muttered complaints. I know how the people mourn this girl, doomed to die the worst of deaths for the noblest of deeds. When her own brother lay slain in battle, unburied, she would not let his body be torn by carrion birds and dogs. "Shouldn't her name," they cry, "be written in gold?" Such are the low murmurs that reach my ear. O father, nothing is more precious to me than your well-being. What higher good can children covet than a father's fair fame, just as fathers too take pride in glorious sons? Therefore, father, don't cling to one mood, and don't think you alone are right and all others wrong. The man who thinks wisdom dwells with him alone, that he alone can speak or think aright — such pronouncements, once tested, turn out to be empty breath. The wisest man will let himself be swayed by others' wisdom and relax in time. See how the trees beside a stream in flood, if they yield to the force, keep every twig unharmed — but by resisting, they perish root and branch. The sailor who keeps his mainsheet taut and won't slacken in a gale is liable to find himself sailing keel-up. Relent, then, and repent of your anger. If a young man may claim some sense, I'll say this: it is best of all to be endowed with absolute wisdom. But if that is denied — and nature is not readily that way inclined — the next best is the man who listens to sage advice.
CHORUS. If he says anything timely, O King, heed him. (To HAEMON.) And you, heed your father too. Both of you have spoken well.
CREON. What — are we at our age to be schooled in prudence by a beardless boy?
HAEMON. I plead for justice, father, nothing more. Weigh me on my merit, not my years.
CREON. A strange merit, to sanction lawlessness!
HAEMON. For evil-doers I would plead no case.
CREON. Is this girl not an arrant law-breaker?
HAEMON. The Theban commons, with one voice, say no.
CREON. What, shall the mob dictate my policy?
HAEMON. It's you, I think, who speak like a boy.
CREON. Am I to rule for others, or for myself?
HAEMON. A state for one man alone is no state at all.
CREON. The state belongs to the one who rules it — so it's held.
HAEMON. As monarch of a desert you would shine.
CREON. This boy, I see, argues the woman's case.
HAEMON. If you are the woman, yes. My concern is for you.
CREON. Reprobate — would you wrangle with your own father?
HAEMON. Because I see you wrongfully perverse.
CREON. And am I wrong to maintain my own rights?
HAEMON. Don't speak of rights. You spurn what Heaven is due.
CREON. O corrupt heart — a woman's minion!
HAEMON. A slave to dishonor you will never find me.
CREON. Your every word has been a plea for her.
HAEMON. And for you, and for me, and for the gods below.
CREON. Living, the girl shall never be your bride.
HAEMON. Then she shall die — but one will die with her.
CREON. Have you come to such a pass as to threaten me?
HAEMON. What threat is it to reprove vain counsels?
CREON. Vain fool, to instruct your betters — you shall rue it.
HAEMON. If you were not my father, I would say you were wrong.
CREON. Don't play the lap-dog, you woman's slave.
HAEMON. When you speak, must no man make reply?
CREON. This goes beyond all bounds! By heaven, you shall not rate and jeer and flout me with impunity. Off with the hateful thing — let her die at once, beside her bridegroom, in his very sight.
HAEMON. Don't think she shall die in my sight, or by my side. Never shall you behold my face again. Go, keep company with friends who can tolerate a madman for their mate.
[Exit HAEMON]

chapters.title: Third Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Your son has gone, my liege, in angry haste. The wrath of youth beneath a sting is fierce indeed.
CREON. Let him go and vent his fury like a fiend. These two sisters he shall not save from death.
CHORUS. Surely you do not mean to kill them both?
CREON. I stand corrected — only her who touched the body.
CHORUS. And what death is she to die?

CREON. She shall be taken to some desert place where no man treads, and in a rock-hewn cave — with just enough food to avoid the blood-guilt that an outright killing might bring on the state — she shall be buried alive. There let her call on the King of Death, the one god she reveres — or learn, at last and too late, that it is wasted labor to reverence the dead.

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: CHORUS. Love, irresistible in fight — all yield at a glance of your eye. Love, who pillows all night long on a maiden's cheek, who ranges over the uplands — shall mortals not yield to you?

All your subjects are mad, and even the wisest heart falls straight into folly at the touch of your poisoned dart. You kindled this strife, this feud of kinsman with kin, by the eyes of a winsome wife, by the longing of her heart to win. For as her consort, enthroned still with Justice above, you bend man to your will, O all-invincible Love.
Look — I myself am swept aside from Justice as I gaze on this bride. (O sight to drown an eye in tears!) Antigone, so young, so fair, hurried down to Death's bower to share the dead.

ANTIGONE. Friends, countrymen, I make my last farewell. My journey is done. One last fond, lingering, longing look I take at the bright sun. For Death, who puts young and old alike to sleep, drags my young life away and beckons me to Acheron's dark fold — an unwed bride. No youths have sung the marriage song for me, no maidens have strewn my bridal bed with meadow flowers. Death is the groom I wed.
CHORUS. But think — you go to the dead great and glorious. You have not tasted the edge of the sword, no disease has wasted your frame. Alive and alone, of your own will, you go down to the dead.

ANTIGONE. No — the piteous tale I have heard men tell of Tantalus' doomed child, chained upon the high rocky crags of Sipylus, clinging like wild ivy, drenched by the pelting rain and whirling snow, left there to pine while on her frozen breast the tears forever flow — her fate is mine.

CHORUS. She was sprung of gods, divine. We are mortals of mortal line. Yet to gain a renown like the gods' is recompense for all your pain. Take this solace with you to the tomb: her fate in life and death is yours.

ANTIGONE. Alas, alas! You mock me. Is it right to insult me to my face while I still live? Stop, I implore you by the altars of our homeland, you lordly rulers of a lordly race. O fount of Dirce, wood-embowered plain where Theban chariots speed to victory — mark the cruel laws that have wrought my ruin, the friends who show no pity in my need! Was ever fate like mine? O monstrous doom — entombed within a rock-built prison, to fade and wither in a living tomb, an alien among both the living and the dead.
CHORUS. In your boldness, over-rash, you dashed your foot madly against the high altar-stair of Justice. You bear a father's guilt.

ANTIGONE. There you touch my most poignant pain — my ill-starred father's piteous disgrace, the taint of blood, the hereditary stain that clings to all of Labdacus' famed race. Alas for the monstrous marriage-bed where a mother lay with the son her own womb had borne. From that I was conceived — alas the day — fruit of incestuous sheets, a forlorn maid. And now I pass, accursed and unwed, to meet them as a stranger in the world below. And you, O brother, ill-fated in your own marriage — it was your dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.

CHORUS. Religion has her claims, it is true. Due rites must be paid when rites are due. Yet it is ill to disobey the powers who by might hold the sway. You withstood authority, a self-willed rebel — and you must die.
ANTIGONE. Unwept, unwed, unfriended, I go, no longer permitted to see the bright eye of day. Not one friend is left to share my bitter sorrow, or to heave one passing sigh over my ashes.

CREON. If wail and lamentation could stave off death, I reckon they would never end. Away with her! Having walled her up in a rock-vaulted tomb, as I ordered, leave her alone, at liberty to die — or, if she prefers, to live in solitude, with the tomb for a dwelling. In either case we are guiltless as regards this maiden's blood. Only — on earth she shall find no lodging.

ANTIGONE. O grave, O bridal chamber, O prison-house hewn from the rock, my everlasting home — where I go to join the mighty host of kinsfolk, Persephassa's guests long dead. I am the last of all, and of all the most miserable, to pass, my destined span of years cut short. And yet I have good hope that I shall find a welcome from my father, a welcome too from you, my mother, and from you, my dear brother. For with my own hands I washed and adorned your limbs in death and poured libations on your graves. And last of all, my Polyneices, to you I paid due rites — and this is my recompense! Yet in wisdom's eyes I am justified. For had it been a child of mine, or a husband moldering in death's decay, I would not have done this deed in defiance of the state. What law do I invoke? This. A husband dead, I might have wed another and borne another child to take the dead child's place. But now that my father and mother are both dead, no second brother can ever be born for me. This was the law of conscience that led me to honor you, dear brother — and by Creon I am judged guilty of a heinous crime. Now he drags me like a criminal, a bride unwed, robbed of the marriage-song, the marriage-bed, and the joys of motherhood — deserted by friends to a living grave. What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed? Hereafter can I look to any god for help, call on any man for aid? Alas, my piety is counted impiety. Well — if such justice is approved by heaven, my sufferings will teach me my sin. But if the sin is theirs, may they suffer no worse ills than the wrongs they have done to me.
CHORUS. The same ungovernable will drives the girl on like a gale.
CREON. Therefore the guards who let her linger shall smart for their delay.
ANTIGONE. Ah, woe is me! This word I hear brings death very near.
CHORUS. I have no comfort. What he says foretells nothing but death.

ANTIGONE. My fatherland, city of Thebes divine, you gods of Thebes from whom my line sprang, look, you mighty lords of Thebes, on me — you see the last of your royal house, martyred by men of sin, undone. Such is the reward my piety has won.
[Exit ANTIGONE]

CHORUS. Like you, that maiden bright, Danae, in her brass-bound tower, once exchanged the glad sunlight for a cell that served as her bridal bower. And yet she sprang of royal line, my child, like yours, and nursed the seed she had conceived of Zeus descending in a golden shower. Strange are the ways of Fate. Her power no wealth withstands, no arms, no tower; nor can bronze-prowed ships that breast the sea flee from Fate.

So too was Dryas' child, the rash Edonian king, brought to a rocky dungeon by Bacchus for his words of high disdain, to cool the madness of a fevered brain. When his frenzy passed, he learned at last that it is madness to hurl gibes at a god. For once he had tried to quench the Maenads' fire, and he provoked the wrath of the tuneful Muses.

By the Iron Rocks that guard the double sea, on the lonely strand of Bosporus, where Salmydessus' plain stretches out in the wild Thracian land, there on his borders Ares witnessed the vengeance taken by a jealous stepmother — the gore that trickled from a spindle red, the sightless sockets of her two stepsons.

Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom, the blasted issue of their mother's womb. But she could trace her lineage to great Erechtheus' race. A daughter of Boreas, reared in her father's vast caves where the tempest rages, swift as his horses she sped over the hills — a child of gods. And yet she too, my child, like you, was vanquished by Destiny, that knows neither death nor age.
[Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
TEIRESIAS. Princes of Thebes, two travelers moving as one — between us we have eyes for one — we are here. The blind man cannot move without a guide.
CREON. What news, old Teiresias?
TEIRESIAS. I will tell you. And when you hear, you must heed the seer.
CREON. So far I have never disobeyed your counsel.
TEIRESIAS. That is why you have steered the ship of state aright.
CREON. I know it, and I gladly own my debt.
TEIRESIAS. Consider — you are treading once again the razor's edge of peril.
CREON. What is this? Your words inspire a dread presentiment.

TEIRESIAS. The divination of my arts will tell you. Sitting at my throne of augury, as is my custom — the place where every bird of heaven finds harborage — I heard on my ears a strange jargon of twitterings, hoots, and screams. So I knew that the birds were tearing at each other with bloody talons, for the whirr of their wings could mean nothing else. Troubled in spirit, I at once attempted the sacrifice by fire on the blazing altars. But the God of Fire did not come in flame. From the thighbones a foul ooze dripped and sputtered in the ashes. Gall-bladders cracked and spurted up. The fat melted and fell away and left the thighbones bare. These signs, which this boy read to me — for as I guide others, so the boy guides me — these were the frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb. O King, your willful temper is the sickness of the state. For all our shrines and altars are defiled by what has filled the maws of dogs and crows — the flesh of Oedipus' unburied son. That is why the angry gods reject our prayers and our burnt offerings. That is why no birds trill a happy note, gorged as they are on the carnival of human gore. O ponder this, my son. To err is common to all men. But the man who, having erred, does not hug his errors but repents and seeks a cure, is not a waster or unwise. As the saying goes, no fool like an obstinate fool. Let death disarm your vengeance. Oh forbear to vex the dead. What glory will you win by killing twice the slain? I mean you well. Counsel that promises gain should be welcome.

CREON. Old man, you all let fly at me with your arrows, as if I were a target. Now you set your soothsayer on me. Peddlers, the whole lot of you — and I the merchandise you buy and sell. Go on — take your profit where you like. Exchange Sardis' silver for the gold of India. You will not purchase this man's burial — not even if the winged ministers of Zeus should bear him in their talons to his throne. Not even in awe of such a dire prodigy would I permit his burial. For I know no human defilement can reach the gods. And this too I know, Teiresias: dire is the fall of craft and cunning when it tries to gloss over foul treachery with fair words for filthy gain.
TEIRESIAS. Alas! Does any man know and lay to heart —
CREON. Is this the prelude to some hackneyed maxim?
TEIRESIAS. How far good counsel is the best of all goods?
CREON. True, as folly is the worst of all ills.
TEIRESIAS. And yet you are infected with that very ill.
CREON. I will not trade insults with you, seer.
TEIRESIAS. And yet you say my prophecies are frauds.
CREON. Prophets are all a money-getting tribe.
TEIRESIAS. And kings are all a lucre-loving race.
CREON. Do you know at whom you glance — me, your lord?
TEIRESIAS. Lord of the state — and savior, thanks to me.
CREON. A skilled prophet, but inclined to wrong.
TEIRESIAS. Take heed — you will provoke me to reveal the mystery deep hidden in my breast.
CREON. Speak on — but see it is not said for gain.
TEIRESIAS. Such, I think, you have judged my words to be, until now.
CREON. Be sure you will not traffic on my wits.

TEIRESIAS. Know then for certain: the coursers of the sun shall not run their race many times more before you shall have given the fruit of your own loins in quittance of your murder, life for life. For you have entombed a living soul, and sent below a denizen of earth, and wronged the nether gods by leaving here a corpse unwashed, unwept, unburied. In this you have no part, nor even the gods in heaven — you usurp a power that is not yours. For this, the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell, who dog the steps of sin, are on your trail. What they have suffered, you shall suffer too. Now consider whether I prophesy for gold. For in a little while the sound of lamentation shall be heard — of men and women through your desolate halls. And all the neighboring states are leagues to avenge their mangled warriors, who have found a grave in the maws of wolves or hounds, or in winged birds that flying home have tainted their city's air. These are the shafts that I, like a bowman provoked to anger, loose at your breast — unerring. Their sting you shall not escape. Boy, lead me home — let him vent his spleen on younger men, and learn to curb his tongue with gentler manners than he has shown today.
[Exit TEIRESIAS]

chapters.title: Fourth Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. My liege, that man has gone, foretelling woe. And believe me, since these grizzled locks of mine were black as a raven's, I have never known the prophet's warning to the state to fail.
CREON. I know it too, and it troubles me. To yield is grievous, but the obstinate soul that fights with Fate is smitten grievously.
CHORUS. Son of Menoeceus, listen to good advice.
CHORUS. What should I do? Advise me — I will heed you.
CHORUS. Go — free the girl from her rocky cell, and build a tomb for the unburied outlaw.
CREON. Is that your counsel? You would have me yield?
CHORUS. Yes, king — this instant. The vengeance of the gods is swift to overtake the impenitent.
CREON. Ah, what a wrench it is to sacrifice my heart's resolve! But Fate is ill to fight.
CHORUS. Go — trust no one else. Do it quickly, yourself.

CREON. I go at once. Bestir yourselves, every one of you, my henchmen! Get axes! Speed to yonder ridge! I too will go. For all my resolve, my mind now sways this way. I was the one who bound her — I too will set her free. Almost I am persuaded it is best to keep through life the laws established of old.
[Exit CREON]
CHORUS. You who are adored by many names, child of Zeus the God of thunder, wonder of a Theban bride, fair guardian of Italy —
In the deep-embosomed glades of the Eleusinian Queen, haunt of revelers, men and maidens, Dionysus, you are seen.
Where Ismenus rolls his waters, where the Dragon's teeth were sown, where the Bacchanals your daughters roam around you — there is your home. Thebes, O Bacchus, is your own.
On the two-crested rock the lurid-flaming torches see you. Where Corycian maidens flock, the springs of Castaly see you too.
By Nysa's bastion clad in ivy, by shores glad with clustered vineyards — there the hymn rings out to you, and through our streets we Thebans shout, All hail to you, Evoe, Evoe!

Oh, since you love this city best of all, to you, and to your Mother struck by lightning, in our dire need we call. You see with what a plague our townsfolk sicken. We crave your ready help, whether you are descending from Parnassus' heights or sweeping over the roaring straits. Save us, O save!

Brightest of all the orbs that breathe forth light, true son of Zeus, immortal king, leader of all the voices of the night — come, and bring with you your train of Thyiads, your maddened rout who dance before you all night long and shout. Your handmaids we, Evoe, Evoe!

chapters.title: Exodos
paragraphs: [Enter MESSENGER]

MESSENGER. Listen, all you who dwell beside the halls of Cadmus and Amphion. No man's life, while it holds its course, could I praise or blame. For Fortune, with her constant ebb and rise, casts down and raises high and low alike — no one can read a mortal's horoscope. Take Creon. He, I thought, if any man, was to be envied. He had saved this land of Cadmus from our enemies, he had attained a monarch's power and ruled the state supreme, while a right noble line of children crowned his happiness. Now it is all gone and wasted. For a life without life's joys I count a living death. You'll say he has ample wealth, the pomp and circumstance of kings. But if these give no pleasure, all the rest I count the shadow of a shadow. I would not weigh all his wealth and power against a dram of joy.
CHORUS. What fresh woes do you bring to the royal house?
MESSENGER. Both are dead — and those who live deserve to die.
CHORUS. Who is the slayer, who the victim? Speak.
MESSENGER. Haemon. His blood shed by no stranger's hand.
CHORUS. What do you mean? By his father's hand or his own?
MESSENGER. His own — in anger at his father's crime.
CHORUS. O prophet, what you foretold has come to pass.
MESSENGER. So the case stands. Now it's for you to act.
CHORUS. Look — from the palace gates I see Creon's unhappy wife, Eurydice, approaching. Is it by chance she comes, or has she heard of her son's fate?
[Enter EURYDICE]

EURYDICE. Men of Thebes, I overheard your talk. As I was passing out to offer up my prayer to Pallas, and was drawing back the bar to open the door wide, there broke upon my ears a wail that told of some household sorrow. Stricken with terror I fainted in the arms of my handmaids. But repeat your tale to one who is no stranger to misery.

MESSENGER. Dear mistress, I was there, and I will tell you the full truth, omitting not a word. Why should we gloze and flatter, only to be proven liars afterward? Truth is always best. Well: in attendance on my lord, your husband, I crossed the plain to its farthest edge, where the corpse of Polyneices, gnawed and mauled, was still lying. We first offered a prayer to Pluto and the goddess of the crossroads, with contrite hearts, to turn away their wrath. Then we washed the mangled corpse with holy water, laid it on fresh-cut branches, lit a pyre, and piled up a great mound of our native earth in his memory. Then to the caverned rock, the bridal chamber of the girl and Death, we hastened, about to enter. But a guard heard a far-off shrill wail from that godless shrine and ran back to our lord to tell the news. As he drew nearer, a hollow sound of lamentation was borne to the king. He groaned and uttered this bitter complaint: "Am I a prophet? Wretched me! Is this the saddest path I have ever trodden? That is my son's voice calling me. On, press on, my henchmen — hurry at double speed to the tomb where the fallen rocks have left a gap. Look in, and tell me whether I truly recognize the voice of Haemon, or whether heaven is deceiving me." So at our distraught lord's bidding we looked, and in the cavern's vaulted gloom I saw the girl hanging dead, strangled in a noose of linen twined about her neck. And close beside her, clasping her cold form, her lover lay, lamenting his dead bride, wedded now to Death, and his father's cruelty. When the King saw him, with a terrible groan he moved toward him, crying, "O my son, what have you done? What came over you? What misfortune has robbed you of your reason? O come out, come out, my son — your father implores you." But the son glared at him with tiger's eyes, spat in his face, and then, without a word, drew his two-hilted sword and struck — but missed, as his father sprang back. Then the boy, enraged with himself, poor wretch, fell on his sword and drove it home through his side. Yet still breathing, he clasped the maiden in his limp arms, her pale cheek turned crimson with his last gasping breaths. So there they lay, two corpses, one in death. His marriage rites are consummated in the halls of Death — a witness that, of all the ills that can befall mortals, their own folly is the worst.
[Exit EURYDICE]
CHORUS. What do you make of this? The Queen has gone without a word, good or ill.

MESSENGER. I marvel too, but I keep good hope. It must be that she shrinks from mourning her son's sad end in public, and wants to lament a private loss in private with her handmaids. Trust me, she is discreet and will not err.
CHORUS. I am not so sure. A strained silence, to my mind, is no less ominous than excessive grief.
MESSENGER. Well — let us go to the house and resolve our doubts, whether the tumult of her heart is concealing some dreadful design. You may be right: unnatural silence bodes no good.
CHORUS. Look — the King himself appears. He carries with him the evidence (ah me, I tremble to bring such a charge against a king) — but all must own the guilt is his, and his alone.

CREON. Woe for the sin of minds perverse, deadly with mortal curse. Behold us, slain and slayers, all of one blood. Woe for my dire counsel, conceived in sin. Alas, my son — your life scarce begun, and you were undone. The fault was mine, mine only, O my son!
CHORUS. Too late, it seems, you perceive the truth.
CREON. I am schooled by sorrow. Heavy is the hand of God. Thorny and rough the paths my feet have trodden. My pride is humbled, my pleasure turned to pain. Poor mortals, how we labor all in vain!
[Enter SECOND MESSENGER]
SECOND MESSENGER. Sorrows are yours, my lord, and more to come. One lies at your feet. Another, more grievous still, waits for you when you reach home.
CREON. What woe is lacking to my tale of woes?
SECOND MESSENGER. Your wife, the mother of your dead son here, lies stricken by a fresh, self-inflicted blow.

CREON. How bottomless the pit! Do you claim me too, O Death? What is this word he says, this woeful messenger? Is it right to slay anew a man already slain? Is Death at work again, stroke upon stroke — first son, then mother slain?
CHORUS. Look for yourself. She lies there for all to see.
CREON. Alas — another woe added before my eyes! What more remains to crown my agony? A minute ago I clasped a lifeless son, and now another victim Death has won. Unhappy mother, most unhappy son!

SECOND MESSENGER. Beside the altar, on a keen-edged sword, she fell and closed her eyes in night. But first she mourned for Megareus, who died nobly long ago, and then for this son. With her last breath she cursed you, the killer of her child.
CREON. I shudder with fright. O for a two-edged sword to slay outright a wretch like me, made one with misery.
SECOND MESSENGER. It is true — you were charged by the dying Queen as the author of both deaths, hers and her son's.
CREON. In what way was her self-destruction wrought?
SECOND MESSENGER. When she heard the loud lament over her son, with her own hand she stabbed herself to the heart.
CREON. I am the guilty cause. I did the deed. I was your murderer. Yes — I plead guilty. My henchmen, lead me away, away — a cipher, less than nothing. No delay!
CHORUS. Well said, if anything in disaster can be well. Present ills demand the speediest cure.
CREON. Come, Fate, a friend in my need — come with all speed! Come, my best friend, and speed my end! Away, away! Let me not look upon another day!
CHORUS. That is for tomorrow. Today has its own needs, and they who must take them in hand must do so.
CREON. I join your prayer — it echoes my own desire.
CHORUS. Oh, pray not — prayers are useless. From the doom fate decrees for mortals, there is no refuge.

CREON. Away with me, a worthless wretch, who unwittingly killed you, my son, and you, his mother too. Where to turn I know not. Every way leads only astray. And on my head I feel the heavy weight of crushing Fate.

CHORUS. The chief part of happiness is a wise heart. To defraud the gods in anything is fraught with peril. Swelling words of high-flown might the gods mightily strike down. Chastisement for errors past brings wisdom to age at last.
